what: A motor drives a Peaucellier linkage: seven moving links and a fixed ground link constrain the red marker to a straight path. Seven moving links make the red marker trace a straight line through a bounded ±60° crank sector, with no sliding guide.
try: Reset and run the example. Watch the blue crank sweep +60°, −60°, then return home.
Pause at an endpoint. Compare the red marker with the fixed origin O; there is no sliding rail.
Change the program to ±30° and predict the shorter stroke before running. Reset first; keep all commands within ±60°.
why: The equal long arms and four equal rhombus sides impose OP × OQ = L² − r². The input point P moves on a circle passing through O. Inversion maps that circle to a straight line, so Q moves vertically although every joint rotates.
matters: Straight-line linkages convert rotation into constrained translation without a sliding guide. Geometry determines both the path and the nonlinear speed along it.
question: Does constant crank speed give constant vertical marker speed?
answer: No. Marker height is proportional to tan(θ/2). Its speed increases toward the endpoints even when the crank turns steadily.
further: Compare the predicted 49.27 mm stroke for ±60° with 22.86 mm for ±30°.
Compare the rack shuttle: its displacement is proportional to shaft angle, unlike this linkage.
formula: L = 80 mm; r = 48 mm; a = OS = SP = 48 mm; xQ = (L² − r²)/(2a) = 42.667 mm; yQ = xQ tan(θ/2)
